power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Random Generation and Reward Exp 4
table.research_questions:
This experiment will be conducted in person, with participants using lab computers via Pavlovia platform. Participants will be presented with six cards, each displaying a value, and will be required either to predict the value of the card to be drawn or to imagine a card being drawn. Subsequently, they will input their predicted or imagined values, both of which will henceforth be referred to as “simulated numbers.” Following the submission of their inputs, the software will play the game and record the outcomes. These outcomes will be employed to determine the amount of the bonus. In the prediction task, the software will evaluate the participants’ predictions against the actual results and present the prediction accuracy.

The experiment includes four independent variables (see “Variables” section for details), and our hypotheses are as follows:
H1: At the group level, participants will generate lower numbers in the loss domain and higher numbers in the gain domain compared to the control domain.
H2: At the individual level, most participants will not be influenced by the domains, with only a few outliers showing domain-related influence.
H3: The instructions for prediction tasks and random generation tasks will not affect the simulated numbers.
H4: Task repetition will influence the simulated numbers:
H4.1: Participants in the one-off condition will simulate more extreme numbers when comparing gain and loss domains against the control condition than in the repeated condition.
H4.2: The simulated number in the one-off condition will be higher than the initial simulated number in the repeated condition.
H5: When simulating numbers repeatedly, participants will show a starting-point bias, with the first simulated number being more extreme than subsequent numbers.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.study_design_overview: This study will employ a 2 (task instruction) x 2 (number of outcomes) x 2 (number of repetitions) x 3 (domains) within-subject design.
table.randomization: We will counterbalance the order of the tasks: half of the participants will start with the random generation task, while the other half will start with the prediction task. Within each task, a Latin square design will be used to balance the order of the 12 conditions.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be recruited through the university's subject pool. Participants will be reimbursed with real money (a participant fee of £5 + a random bonus) for their time to take part in the experiment. The bonus ranges from £0 to £20, and the average value of the bonus is £10.
table.sample_size: Our target sample size is 48 participants, or as many as we can before September 30, 2024.
table.stopping_rule: We will stop data collection once the sample size reaches 48 or by September 30, 2024, whichever comes first.
table.manipulated_variables:
The variables are as follows:
• Task
     • Prediction task: Participants predict the value of gambles.
     • Random generation task: Participants imagine the value if gambles are played.
• Number of repetitions
     • One-off: Participants complete the task once.
     • Repeated: Participants complete the task ten times consecutively.
• Number of outcomes
     • Two outcomes: The gamble has two outcomes: three cards assigned a value of 0, and the other three cards assigned a value of 5;
     • Six outcomes: The gamble has six outcomes: each card displaying a number ranging from 0 to 5;
• Domain
     • Control: The outcomes of the gamble are plain numbers;
     • Gain: The outcomes of the gambles are winning money (in pounds sterling);
     • Loss: The outcomes of the gambles are losing money (in pounds sterling).
table.measured_variables: We will record the participants’ simulated numbers. There will be 132 numbers in total.
table.statistical_tests: We will analyse the data at both the group and individual levels. The main methods we are going to employ will be Bayesian ANOVA (`BayesFactor::anovaBF`) and inclusion log Bayes Factor (logBF; `bayestestR::bf_inclusion()`). Please see the attached file "Exp 4 - analysis plan.md" for more details. 66b76885b2501c61cd5da5d5 Exp 4 - analysis plan.md https://osf.io/project/sbeq9/files/osfstorage/66b76885b2501c61cd5da5d5 https://osf.io/download/66b76885b2501c61cd5da5d5 cbce05c142000b933bac21e1dba04380b72ebb99ea9c7d9a6cb77c4656baf76b
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
The participants who meet any of the following three criteria will be excluded from the analysis:
• If a participant has more than 13 invalid and missing inputs in total, the participant’s data will be excluded;
• Participants who fail both of the comprehension checks about the task instructions will be excluded;
• We will use the measure of determinism (DET; Marwan et al., 2007; Webber Jr & Zbilut, 1994) in the Recurrence quantification analysis and apply it to the numbers simulated in the two-outcome–repeated–control and six-outcome–repeated–control conditions. The minimum length for DET will be set to two, and participants with at least one DET equal to or higher than 0.9 will be excluded.

References
Marwan, N., Carmenromano, M., Thiel, M., & Kurths, J. (2007). Recurrence plots for the analysis of complex systems. Physics Reports, 438(5–6), 237–329. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physrep.2006.11.001
Webber Jr, C. L., & Zbilut, J. P. (1994). Dynamical assessment of physiological systems and states using recurrence plot strategies. Journal of Applied Physiology, 76(2), 965–973.
table.additional_comments:
We will include three comprehension checks throughout the study. The first check will occur after the instruction on how the bonus is calculated. Participants should understand that neither their answers nor their performance will influence the bonus. The remaining two checks will be placed at the end of each task to evaluate participants’ understanding of the task instructions. These will be a forced choice question: “Which task have you been asked to do?” with two options provided: “imagine drawing cards” and “predict cards to be drawn”.

The incentive will be real money and will vary across participants. Participants will be reimbursed with real money (£5 + a random bonus) for taking part in the experiment. The bonus will range from £0 to £20, with an expected value of £10. Participants will be endowed with £10 at the beginning of the experiment. At the end of the experiment, the program will randomly select one outcome from each type of the six games (reflecting three domains and two outcome numbers).

The endowment will be adjusted according to the results of the gambles, so participants may gain or lose some of the money.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 492 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (8), version control (484). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1440 columns across 56 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 56 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: In this task, participants were presented with a deck of cards containing both blank and marked cards.
Participants were informed of the exact proportion before the trial and, for each proportion, made a single prediction about whether a randomly drawn card would be marked or blank.

Participants were more likely to predict a marked card in the desirable condition and less likely in the undesirable condition compared to the neutral scenario (Irwin, 1953; Marks, 1951; see also Krizan and Windschitl, 2007 for a review).

Similar to the Marks paradigm, in which participants are asked for a single prediction of a lottery, random generation asks participants to imagine playing lotteries, for example, by imagining drawing a slip of paper with a number, reporting it, replacing it, shuffling, and repeating the process.

Critically, we manipulated the meaning of these values such that in one condition, participants were told they would represent winning points, in another losing points, or else were described simply as numbers (i.e., not associated with winning or losing).
All participants were recruited via the University of Warwick participant pool (https://warwick.sona-systems.com/).
Participants were reimbursed with Amazon vouchers (a show-up fee of £3 and a random bonus).
In each domain, participants were presented with a set of 11 slips of paper of identical size representing the numbers 0 to 10.

Participants were asked to imagine "drawing a slip out from a bag, saying the number or the outcome on it out loud, putting it back, shuffling, then repeating the process", following the instructions in Baddeley (1966).
Importantly, in the gain and loss domains, participants were asked to articulate the full phrase "winning" or "losing [x] points" during every response to ensure they did not forget the domain.
Participants were then asked to generate draws from that set as spoken responses for four minutes.
To maintain a consistent response pace, participants were asked to open a web page with a purple dot flashing at the centre of the screen, 37 beats per minute.
Participants were asked to generate a number every time the dot appeared.
Two participants were excluded due to generating at least one sequence that was shorter than 80% of the required length (i.e., fewer than 118 numbers).
In the loss domain, participants were endowed with 10 points before the gamble, so they would not truly lose points.

Directionally, participants were optimistic in random generation, showing the lowest mean values in the loss domain (M loss = 4.83), followed by the control domain 279 (M control = 5.01), and the gain domain (M gain = 5.42).
The individual RM-BANOVAs reveal which participants were affected by outcome utility, but the direction of bias among the affected participants remained unclear.

Under Neutrality, participants are expected to sample from the neutral distribution, the histogram of the random generation in the control domain, meaning that random generation results in the control domain should generalise across all domains (represented by the distribution of Random generation in the left panel of Figure 3).

Further individual-level analyses confirmed that the majority of the participants were unaffected by the utilities and drew samples from the same distribution, regardless of whether they were placed within the control, gain or loss The comparison between the empirical and hypothetical distributions in the gain and loss domains in Experiment 1.
These analyses did however also find a small minority of participants were seemingly influenced by utility, potentially indicating some individual differences in effects.

The design and procedure were identical to Experiment 1 (Figure 2), with the following exceptions: participants were asked to have both the microphone and the camera on, and their video and voice were recorded.
Participants were presented with ten coins in a transparent box.
The order of the domains was counterbalanced as we did in Experiment 1, and the participants were still asked to follow a flashing dot at a pace of 37 times per minute.
Then the participants were given a T/20 chance to win a £1 bonus or otherwise only received the show-up fee.

Three participants were excluded due to generating at least one sequence that was shorter than 80% of the required length (i.e., fewer than 118 numbers); one participant was excluded due to having more than three values outside of the range of 0 and 10.

Overall, 72% of the participants (26 out of 36, 95% CI = [54.81%, 85.80%]) fell within the ellipse, while five participants were in the Centralisation region, two in the Polarisation region, and three in the Optimism region.
A second difference lies in the task instructions: participants were asked to imagine drawing a card in the random generation task and to predict which card would be drawn in the Marks paradigm.
A total of 154 participants (132 women, 20 men, 2 other; age: M = 18.7 years, SD = 0.8) were recruited via the University of Warwick's subject pool.

This approach created 24 possible condition orders, and we ensured that the number of participants assigned to each order was as balanced as possible, with the difference in sample size across orders kept to no more than one.
Participants were shown a figure of six cards.
At the start of each condition, participants were introduced to the gamble, where the cards would be shuffled, and a random card drawn with replacement.
In the random generation task, participants were instructed to imagine drawing a card, while in the prediction task, participants were asked to predict the value on a randomly drawn card.
After the instruction screen, participants had 30 seconds to enter their imagined or predicted value in a text box and click the "Next" button to continue.

Although no monetary rewards were used, participants were given 220 points at the beginning of the experiment to establish a context of winning and losing, and they viewed their aggregated results at the end.

The results indicate that the majority of participants were unaffected by the variables: 78% for the domains (76 out of 98, CI = [68.01%, 85.36%]), 70% for the repetition (69 out of 98, 95% CI = [60.34%, 79.21%]), and 84% for their interaction (82 out of 98, 95% CI = [74.84%, 90.37%]).
To avoid the correlation being artificially caused by individual points clustering in a small area, participants were categorised based on their individual BFs, using a comparison threshold of 1/3.
The group-level RM-BANOVA revealed an optimistic bias, whereas the individual-level RM-BANOVA indicated that 63% of participants were uninfluenced by the domains.
For the manipulation of the experimental design, we found that participants were not influenced by task instruction or the number of outcomes, but were affected by repetition.

In similar studies, participants are often rewarded for accuracy (e.g., Budescu & Bruderman, 1995; Crandall et al., 1955) or receive feedback, such as being shown the actual results after making their predictions (e.g., Park et al., 2022).
We recruited 48 participants (25 women, 23 men; age: M =24.8 years, SD=3.0) via the University of Warwick subject pool (https://warwick.sona-systems.com/).
The 24 condition orders were counterbalanced, with two participants assigned to each order.
The participants were initially given a cash note of £10, which was put in front of them throughout the experiment and could gain or lose from it depending on the results of the gambles.
We also preregistered an exclusion criterion based on DET, whereby participants with DET exceeding 90% in any of the repeated-control conditions would be excluded.

The following analyses therefore omitted this criterion, though for transparency, we report analyses using the originally planned exclusion criteria in Appendix G, which yielded a sample size of 15 participants.

The BFs for the two-and six-outcome conditions were found to be significantly and positively correlated (Pearson correlation coefficient after Box-Cox transformation: r(38) = .78, p < .001). 6 To further analyse this, participants were categorised based on their individual BFs, using a comparison threshold of 1/3.
Additionally, 10 and 14 participants were classified under the UWS models with k = 1, u = u(0) and k = 0.5, u = u(0), respectively.

However, we observed the same pattern as in Experiments 1 and 3: Optimistic participants were assigned to U-shaped importance distributions that failed to capture their optimistic tendencies but still yielded the highest overall likelihood.

Further individual-level analyses revealed a clear shift from Experiment 3 to Experiment 4: whereas most participants were not influenced by domain in Experiment 3, the majority were influenced in Experiment 4.

The results indicate that 1591 the majority of participants were unaffected by the variables: 67% for the domains (99 out 1592 of 147, CI = [59.13%, 74.85%]), 59% for the repetition (87 out of 147, 95% CI = [50.78%, 1593 67.21%]), and 74% for their interaction (109 out of 147, 95% CI = [66.29%, 81.01%]).

text.text: Data sets, analysis scripts and the experimental programs are available online on the Open Science Framework at https://osf.io/sn5k2.
text.formatted: Data sets, analysis scripts and the experimental programs are available online on the Open Science Framework at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/sn5k2">https://osf.io/sn5k2</ref>.

text.text: Experiment 4 is preregistered on the Open Science Framework at https://osf.io/sbeq9.

text.text: Imagine participating in a raffle where the total number of tickets and the number of winning tickets are known.
How do you perceive your chances of winning?
The subjective representations of probabilities play a crucial role in how we understand and navigate uncertainty.
Current research suggests that humans do not directly represent or calculate probabilities (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973).
text.formatted: Current research suggests that humans do not directly represent or calculate probabilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Kahneman & Tversky, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: Instead, this process is more likely implemented through a sampling mechanism (Sanborn & Chater, 2016), which can be viewed as mentally simulating the possible consequences of an uncertain event (Hotaling, 2020; Lieder et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Instead, this process is more likely implemented through a sampling mechanism <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Sanborn & Chater, 2016)</ref>, which can be viewed as mentally simulating the possible consequences of an uncertain event <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hotaling, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lieder et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Sampling-based accounts have been developed for both probability judgments (e.g., Costello & Watts, 2014 , 2016 , 2017; Zhu et al., 2020 Zhu et al., , 2024) ) and risky choice (e.g., Bhatia, 2014; Busemeyer & Diederich, 2002; Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993; Lieder et al., 2018), and have been successful in characterising cognitive processes and explaining a range of robust effects in judgment and decision making.
text.formatted: Sampling-based accounts have been developed for both probability judgments (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Costello & Watts, 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Zhu et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Zhu et al., , 2024) )</ref> and risky choice (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bhatia, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Busemeyer & Diederich, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lieder et al., 2018)</ref>, and have been successful in characterising cognitive processes and explaining a range of robust effects in judgment and decision making.

text.text: Despite their success, existing sampling-based theories make different assumptions about how outcome utility interacts with the probability of being sampled, and there is little direct evidence on how people mentally simulate outcomes that differ in utility.
Consider a gamble with a 50/50 chance of winning £5 or nothing.
One possibility is that people simulate the two outcomes in roughly equal proportion; another is that they generate £5 more or less often than would be expected from the objective probabilities.
This raises an important question: Do explicit utilities influence the probabilities with which outcomes are mentally sampled, and if so, in what ways do they shape this sampling process?

Allowing for two possible directions of bias (undersampling or oversampling) in two differing domains (gains and losses), we can outline four potential biased hypotheses and one unbiased neutrality hypothesis, as illustrated in Figure 1.
text.formatted: Allowing for two possible directions of bias (undersampling or oversampling) in two differing domains (gains and losses), we can outline four potential biased hypotheses and one unbiased neutrality hypothesis, as illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: According to many sequential sampling models of decision-making (e.g., Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993; Krajbich et al., 2010 Krajbich et al., , 2012;; Zilker & Pachur, 2021), outcomes are sampled in proportion to their probabilities, with utility showing no influence on the process.
text.formatted: According to many sequential sampling models of decision-making (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Krajbich et al., 2010</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Krajbich et al., , 2012;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Zilker & Pachur, 2021)</ref>, outcomes are sampled in proportion to their probabilities, with utility showing no influence on the process.

text.text: This is the Neutrality hypothesis.
However, little empirical evidence has been found to support it.
By contrast, several theories and empirical findings suggest that sampling may be systematically biased by outcomes' utility.
Hypothesised patterns of mental sampling as a function of outcome domain and sampling bias, with corresponding theoretical accounts shown in brackets.

As proposed by the risk-reward heuristic (Pleskac & Hertwig, 2014), when outcome values are provided but the associated probabilities are not, people's judgments often reflect utility-based beliefs derived from their environment.
text.formatted: As proposed by the risk-reward heuristic <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Pleskac & Hertwig, 2014)</ref>, when outcome values are provided but the associated probabilities are not, people's judgments often reflect utility-based beliefs derived from their environment.

text.text: For instance, larger gains, such as national lotteries, are generally less common than smaller gains.
Under these conditions, a Centralisation bias might emerge.

Supporting this, Pleskac and Hertwig (2014) and Hoffart et al. (2019) found that, under uncertainty, people tended to assign lower probability to higher reward, believing that larger rewards were less likely than smaller ones.
text.formatted: Supporting this, <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Pleskac and Hertwig (2014)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hoffart et al. (2019)</ref> found that, under uncertainty, people tended to assign lower probability to higher reward, believing that larger rewards were less likely than smaller ones.

text.text: While not empirically tested in these studies, Pleskac and Hertwig (2014) argued that people would, in line with the notion of a fair bet, think that larger losses would be less likely than smaller losses.
text.formatted: While not empirically tested in these studies, <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Pleskac and Hertwig (2014)</ref> argued that people would, in line with the notion of a fair bet, think that larger losses would be less likely than smaller losses.

text.text: Thus, if mental simulations are guided by prior beliefs, particularly when outcome distributions are not explicitly provided, we would expect to observe a Centralisation bias.

Alternatively, from a resource-rational perspective, decision-making under limited sampling may benefit from focusing on outcomes with the greatest absolute utility. Lieder et al. (2018) argued that in such cases, preferential sampling of outcomes with the greatest absolute utility difference from the mean outcome can improve the quality of the decision.
text.formatted: Alternatively, from a resource-rational perspective, decision-making under limited sampling may benefit from focusing on outcomes with the greatest absolute utility. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lieder et al. (2018)</ref> argued that in such cases, preferential sampling of outcomes with the greatest absolute utility difference from the mean outcome can improve the quality of the decision.

text.text: For example, in Russian roulette, decision-making improves if the decision maker prioritises sampling the fatal outcome, ensuring this possibility is not overlooked.
This idea is formalised in the Utility-Weighted Sampling (UWS, Lieder et al., 2018) model, which predicts oversampling of extreme outcomes, namely the largest gains and losses.
text.formatted: This idea is formalised in the Utility-Weighted Sampling (UWS, <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lieder et al., 2018)</ref> model, which predicts oversampling of extreme outcomes, namely the largest gains and losses.

text.text: This prediction is consistent with empirical findings showing that extreme outcomes were recalled first and at rates higher than their objective probabilities (Ludvig et al., 2014; Madan et al., 2014 Madan et al., , 2021)).
text.formatted: This prediction is consistent with empirical findings showing that extreme outcomes were recalled first and at rates higher than their objective probabilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Ludvig et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Madan et al., 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Madan et al., , 2021))</ref>.

text.text: We refer to this pattern as the Polarisation hypothesis.

People may also be influenced by defensive pessimism (Norem & Cantor, 1986), in which individuals deliberately lower their expectations to prepare for potential disappointment and to protect self-esteem in the face of possible failure.
text.formatted: People may also be influenced by defensive pessimism <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Norem & Cantor, 1986)</ref>, in which individuals deliberately lower their expectations to prepare for potential disappointment and to protect self-esteem in the face of possible failure.

text.text: The evidence comes from a probability judgment task in Experiment 2 of de Molière and Harris's study (2016), where participants estimated the probability of three risky events that shared the same objective probability but differed in their outcomes: gaining money, losing money, or a neutral condition with no monetary consequences.
text.formatted: The evidence comes from a probability judgment task in Experiment 2 of de Molière and Harris's study <ref type="bibr">(2016)</ref>, where participants estimated the probability of three risky events that shared the same objective probability but differed in their outcomes: gaining money, losing money, or a neutral condition with no monetary consequences.

text.text: Their findings showed that, compared to the neutral condition, probability estimates were higher in the loss-money scenario and lower in the gain-money scenario (shown in their Figure 2).
text.formatted: Their findings showed that, compared to the neutral condition, probability estimates were higher in the loss-money scenario and lower in the gain-money scenario (shown in their Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>).

text.text: Viewed in this way, the mental simulations may, at least under some conditions, be biased towards the Pessimism hypothesis.
Finally, the desirability bias (Krizan & Windschitl, 2007) reflects the influence of our desires on our expectations of the future, which is consistent with Optimism.
text.formatted: Finally, the desirability bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Krizan & Windschitl, 2007)</ref> reflects the influence of our desires on our expectations of the future, which is consistent with Optimism.

text.text: Most of this evidence comes from the "Marks paradigm" (Marks, 1951).
text.formatted: Most of this evidence comes from the "Marks paradigm" <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Marks, 1951)</ref>.

text.text: In this task, participants were presented with a deck of cards containing both blank and marked cards.
The proportion of marked cards varied between 10% and 90%.
Participants were informed of the exact proportion before the trial and, for each proportion, made a single prediction about whether a randomly drawn card would be marked or blank.
The marked card could take on one of three meanings depending on the scenario: winning a point (desirable condition), losing a point (undesirable condition), or being meaningless (neutral condition).

Participants were more likely to predict a marked card in the desirable condition and less likely in the undesirable condition compared to the neutral scenario (Irwin, 1953; Marks, 1951; see also Krizan and Windschitl, 2007 for a review).
text.formatted: Participants were more likely to predict a marked card in the desirable condition and less likely in the undesirable condition compared to the neutral scenario <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Irwin, 1953;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Marks, 1951</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Krizan and Windschitl, 2007</ref> for a review).

text.text: Taken together, these literatures outline five plausible theoretical directions for how utilities might shape mental simulations.

However, the empirical studies implying the theories differ in paradigms, and none directly investigates the sequence of simulated outcomes that is central to many decision theories (e.g., Hotaling, 2020; Lieder et al., 2018).
text.formatted: However, the empirical studies implying the theories differ in paradigms, and none directly investigates the sequence of simulated outcomes that is central to many decision theories (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hotaling, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lieder et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, individual differences have received limited attention in these studies.
Most of them focus on testing broad hypotheses using group means, which can obscure variability among participants.

Our aim is to place these suggestive findings within a unified sampling framework and test them at both the group and individual levels, using a paradigm that elicits repeated simulations, namely, the random generation task (Baddeley, 1966).
text.formatted: Our aim is to place these suggestive findings within a unified sampling framework and test them at both the group and individual levels, using a paradigm that elicits repeated simulations, namely, the random generation task <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Baddeley, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: Similar to the Marks paradigm, in which participants are asked for a single prediction of a lottery, random generation asks participants to imagine playing lotteries, for example, by imagining drawing a slip of paper with a number, reporting it, replacing it, shuffling, and repeating the process.
Both tasks require generating outcomes, but the random generation task explicitly involves a repeated sampling process.

The paradigm has also been applied to explore the mental sampling process in other domains, such as stereotypes (Falbén et al., 2024), and events with equal and unequal probabilities (Castillo et al., 2024 (Castillo et al., , 2026;; León-Villagrá et al., 2026; Spicer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The paradigm has also been applied to explore the mental sampling process in other domains, such as stereotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Falbén et al., 2024)</ref>, and events with equal and unequal probabilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Castillo et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Castillo et al., , 2026;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">León-Villagrá et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Spicer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These features make this paradigm well-suited to examining the mental simulation process.

Building on this, we designed four experiments that used the random generation task to directly test whether and how utilities influence the mental simulation of risky events when the outcomes and probabilities are specified.
In these experiments, we asked participants to imagine playing a gamble repeatedly, and then say out loud or write down the outcome they imagined.
We also collected responses of probability judgments (Experiments 1 and 2) and predictions (Experiments 3 and 4) and compared them with random generation's results.

Critically, we manipulated the meaning of these values such that in one condition, participants were told they would represent winning points, in another losing points, or else were described simply as numbers (i.e., not associated with winning or losing).
The first two experiments employed random generation with different probability distributions.

Experiment 1 involved a uniform distribution, represented by drawing slips of paper from a bag, whereas Experiment 2 employed a binomial distribution, illustrated by counting the number of heads after simultaneously tossing ten coins.
In both experiments, we also obtained probability judgments to compare aggregated beliefs with the distributions of generated outcomes.
Experiments 3 and 4 aimed to test the generalizability of the findings from the first two experiments.

Specifically, in Experiment 3, we used a drawing-card scenario based on the Marks paradigm to evaluate whether our findings in Experiments 1 and 2 were driven by specific materials, procedures, or, most importantly, the task instruction (random generation vs. prediction).
Using a similar program as Experiment 3, we conducted Experiment 4 in the laboratory with more salient monetary contexts to test the boundary conditions of the findings.
In Experiment 1, we employed the random generation paradigm to investigate how participants mentally simulate a gamble with equally probable outcomes.
The experiment included three domains: gains, losses, and a neutral control condition.
Our primary objective was to determine whether the utility influences the generated results.
A total of 30 participants (8 women, 22 men; age: M = 22.0 years, SD = 3.6) took part in the study.
The sample size was chosen to be consistent with previous studies using similar random generation designs (e.g., Castillo et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The sample size was chosen to be consistent with previous studies using similar random generation designs (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Castillo et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: All participants were recruited via the University of Warwick participant pool (https://warwick.sona-systems.com/).
text.formatted: All participants were recruited via the University of Warwick participant pool (<ref type="url" target="https://warwick.sona-systems.com/">https://warwick.sona-systems.com/</ref>).

text.text: Participants were reimbursed with Amazon vouchers (a show-up fee of £3 and a random bonus).
The bonus ranged from 0p to 20p, and the expected value of the bonus is 10p.
Ethical approval was given by the Humanities and Social Sciences Research Ethics Committee (HSSREC) at the University of Warwick.
The experiment employed a within-subjects design, incorporating three variants of a random generation task through three distinct domains: gain, loss, and control.
All the participants began with the control domain, and the order of the subsequent gain and loss domains was counterbalanced across subjects.
In each domain, participants were presented with a set of 11 slips of paper of identical size representing the numbers 0 to 10.

Domains differed in the value of these numbers: In the gain domain, slips were labeled as "winning [x] points"; in the loss domain, slips were labeled as "losing [x] points", where "x" represents each of the numbers 0 to 10; in the control domain, slips were only labeled with their respective number.

Participants were asked to imagine "drawing a slip out from a bag, saying the number or the outcome on it out loud, putting it back, shuffling, then repeating the process", following the instructions in Baddeley (1966).
text.formatted: Participants were asked to imagine "drawing a slip out from a bag, saying the number or the outcome on it out loud, putting it back, shuffling, then repeating the process", following the instructions in <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Baddeley (1966)</ref>.

text.text: To help participants understand the instructions, the experimenter visually illustrated the process without revealing the slip contents.
Importantly, in the gain and loss domains, participants were asked to articulate the full phrase "winning" or "losing [x] points" during every response to ensure they did not forget the domain.
The experiment was conducted in a one-to-one online meeting using Microsoft Teams, and participants' audio was recorded.
The main procedure is shown in Figure 2.
text.formatted: The main procedure is shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>.

text.text: The experiment contained three blocks, one for each of the three domains.

At the start of a block, the experimenter displayed a photograph of the set of slips for that domain and demonstrated the raffle by placing the slips into a bag, shaking it, and drawing one out without revealing its label.
The instructions were: "Please imagine this task repeatedly.
Each time, I will shake the bag, draw a slip, and you imagine the number or outcome on it.
Then I will put the slip back, shuffle the bag, and repeat the process."
Participants were then asked to generate draws from that set as spoken responses for four minutes.
To maintain a consistent response pace, participants were asked to open a web page with a purple dot flashing at the centre of the screen, 37 beats per minute.
Participants were asked to generate a number every time the dot appeared.
They produced responses slightly faster than requested, producing an average sequence length of 155.71 numbers (SD = 27.82).

At the end of each block, participants received a questionnaire with two questions: first, a forced-choice question, whether all the numbers were equally likely; and second, the probabilities of each number as a percentage without requiring that they sum to 100.
After the questionnaire, in the gain and loss domains, the experimenter drew a slip from a bag in front of the participants.
The outcome on the slip was not revealed until the end of the experiment and was either added to or subtracted from the point total.
This total was then converted into a cash bonus, with each point equaling one penny.
1 This approach aimed to encode outcomes as either losses or gains while keeping them independent from the random generation tasks.
The experiment took about 40 minutes to complete.
Two participants were excluded due to generating at least one sequence that was shorter than 80% of the required length (i.e., fewer than 118 numbers).
The results reported below are for the final sample of 28 participants.

When analysing and reporting the data, each generated response was converted into its absolute value, meaning "5" in the control domain, "winning 5 points" in the gain domain, and "losing 5 points" in the loss domain were all transcribed as 5 (and all termed "number" below).

Our analyses consist of four parts: examination of participants' understanding of the probabilities, consistency between generation and judgment, group-level utility effects, and individual differences.
The analyses of utility effects primarily used repeated-measures Bayesian ANOVA (RM-BANOVA), implemented in the BayesFactor package in R (version 0.9.12-4.7; Morey et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The analyses of utility effects primarily used repeated-measures Bayesian ANOVA (RM-BANOVA), implemented in the BayesFactor package in R (version 0.9.12-4.7; <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Morey et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Default prior scales were applied.
And when RM-BANOVA 1 The concept of converting points to money, and the minimum and maximum win, were explained to the participants at the beginning of the experiment.
However, the actual conversion was not revealed until the experiment was over.
In the loss domain, participants were endowed with 10 points before the gamble, so they would not truly lose points.

was applied at the group-level, the maximal random-effects structure of subjects was specified, including random intercepts and slopes for all variables to account for individual variability (Oberauer, 2022; van den Bergh et al., 2023).
text.formatted: was applied at the group-level, the maximal random-effects structure of subjects was specified, including random intercepts and slopes for all variables to account for individual variability <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Oberauer, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">van den Bergh et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Inclusion Bayes factors (BFs) were then calculated using the bayestestR package (version 0.13.2; Makowski et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Inclusion Bayes factors (BFs) were then calculated using the bayestestR package (version 0.13.2; <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Makowski et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: All RM-BANOVAs were performed on the raw response numbers, and analyses based on mean values are explicitly indicated in the text.
We first checked participants' explicit understanding of the objective probabilities.

For the forced choice question, the majority of participants selected "equal" across the three domains: 79% in the control domain (22 out of 28, 95% CI = [59.05%, 91.70%]), 68% in the gain domain (19 out of 28, 95% CI = [47.65%, 84.12%]), and 82% in the loss domain (23 out of 28, 95% CI = [63.11%, 93.94%]).
Detailed counts are presented in Table 1.
text.formatted: Detailed counts are presented in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, we conducted a comparison of the proportion of "equal" responses in the gain and loss domains relative to the control domain.

Using McNemar's test with continuity correction, we were unable to reject the null hypothesis, which states participants report the same pattern of probability based on our manipulation of the gain or loss domain.
Specifically, the test results were χ 2 (1, N = 28) = 1.33, p = .5 for the control-gain comparison and χ 2 (1, N = 28) = 1, p = 1 for the control-loss comparison, after a Holm-Bonferroni correction.
In this analysis, we wanted to investigate whether explicit judgments align with implicit simulation.
We first compared the aggregate distributions obtained from the two tasks.
Figure 3 illustrates the distribution of (normalised) probability judgments and random generation proportions across numbers for each domain.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref> illustrates the distribution of (normalised) probability judgments and random generation proportions across numbers for each domain.

text.text: To obtain these two types of distributions, we normalised the probability judgments and the histogram of the random generation for each participant and calculated the mean value for each number across the participants.

Comparisons with the uniform distribution via one-sample t tests and Holm-Bonferroni correction, as shown in Figure 3, revealed tendencies to under-generate 0 in the loss domain, under-generate 0 and 1 in the gain domain, and over-generate 3 in the loss domain.
text.formatted: Comparisons with the uniform distribution via one-sample t tests and Holm-Bonferroni correction, as shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>, revealed tendencies to under-generate 0 in the loss domain, under-generate 0 and 1 in the gain domain, and over-generate 3 in the loss domain.

text.text: Furthermore, we observed high similarity between the probability judgment and random generation distributions, quantified by the overlapping index (Pastore & Calcagnì, 2019; Weitzman, 1970), measuring the percentage of these distributions covering the same area; overlapping indices were calculated individually for each subject, and the mean coefficient for each domain is presented in Figure 3.
text.formatted: Furthermore, we observed high similarity between the probability judgment and random generation distributions, quantified by the overlapping index <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Pastore & Calcagnì, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Weitzman, 1970)</ref>, measuring the percentage of these distributions covering the same area; overlapping indices were calculated individually for each subject, and the mean coefficient for each domain is presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>.

text.text: Next, we examined whether participants' probability judgments and random generation responses were correlated across tasks in terms of their distributional means and variances within each domain.
Consistency across tasks would predict positive correlations for both measures.
The results, summarised in Table 2, include Pearson's correlation coefficients and the corresponding p-values and BFs.
text.formatted: The results, summarised in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>, include Pearson's correlation coefficients and the corresponding p-values and BFs.

text.text: These analyses, however, did not indicate any significant correlations between the two tasks.
In this analysis, we addressed our main question: whether utility influenced participants' responses.
If utility had such an influence, we would expect the mean responses to differ across the domains.

Directionally, participants were optimistic in random generation, showing the lowest  mean values in the loss domain (M loss = 4.83), followed by the control domain 279 (M control = 5.01), and the gain domain (M gain = 5.42).

However, an RM-BANOVA on the 280 random generation data, with domain as the fixed effect and participants as the random intercepts and slopes, provided substantial evidence against a domain effect (BF = 1/3.48).

In contrast, probability judgments showed a pessimistic pattern, with the lowest mean in the gain domain (M gain = 4.96), followed by the control domain (M control = 5.04) and the loss domain (M loss = 5.21).
The descriptive trends suggest that the two tasks may differ in how outcome utility influences responses.

To test this possibility, we conducted an RM-BANOVA comparing random generation means and probability judgment means, with domain, task (random generation versus probability judgment) and their interaction as factors.
The BFs provided anecdotal evidence for effects of domain (BF = 2.19) and task (BF = 2.03), and substantial evidence for an interaction (BF = 7.57).
The higher BF for domains compared with the earlier analysis likely reflects the use of aggregated means per participant rather than raw responses.
A similar pattern was reported in Table 1 of Oberauer (2022), where the BFs based on the aggregated data tended to be larger than those based on the unaggregated data.
text.formatted: A similar pattern was reported in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> of <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Oberauer (2022)</ref>, where the BFs based on the aggregated data tended to be larger than those based on the unaggregated data.

text.text: This is mainly because unaggregated data provide many more observations, allowing more precise estimation of the random effects and a clearer separation between random and fixed effects.
The group-level BF for domains supports the neutrality hypothesis in Figure 1.
text.formatted: The group-level BF for domains supports the neutrality hypothesis in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: However, this might be because biases are inconsistent across individuals and may cancel out when averaged.
To examine whether this pattern held at the individual level, we next analysed participants separately.
This approach allowed us to identify whether the apparent neutrality at the group level reflected a consistent tendency across individuals.
The individual-level analysis consisted of three parts.

First, because each participant generated a long sequence of numbers in every domain, we had sufficient observations to run an RM-BANOVA on each participant's data and quantify the domain effect at the individual level.
We then visualised each participant's response by locating them within the five regions shown in Figure 1.
text.formatted: We then visualised each participant's response by locating them within the five regions shown in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: Finally, we conducted a quantitative distribution-based evaluation to determine which hypothesis best fitted each participant's random generation distribution.
Individual RM-BANOVA.
We first tested whether utility had any detectable effect at the individual level, without assuming a common direction of bias across participants.
To do so, we applied an RM-BANOVA to each participant's data.
Table A1 shows the distribution of the individual BF.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">A1</ref> shows the distribution of the individual BF.

text.text: We found that 79% of the participants (22 out of 28, 95% CI = [59.05%, 91.70%]) had a BF value below 1/3, indicating that the majority were not influenced by the domains.
Visualisation.
The individual RM-BANOVAs reveal which participants were affected by outcome utility, but the direction of bias among the affected participants remained unclear.
We therefore next examined the direction of each participant's bias (or the absence of bias), with the aim of placing each individual into one of the five regions illustrated in Figure 1.

text.text: The first step was to use the control domain as the baseline for comparison with the gain and loss domains.

We calculated the mean values of each domain for each participant, and then subtracted the mean value of the control domain from the mean values of the gain and the loss domains: If extreme values are oversampled in the signed domains, the mean response should exceed that in the control condition.
Figure 4 shows the relationship between the empirical M gain -M control and M loss -M control at the individual level.

text.text: To identify participants whose responses were consistent with Neutrality, we constructed an ellipse representing the range of mean differences expected under utility-independent sampling.

We found that 82% of the participants (23 out of 28, 95% CI = [63.11%, 93.94%]), including all 22 participants whose individual BF of the domains were below 1/3, had points that fell within the ellipse.
This indicates that the majority of participants showed patterns consistent with Neutrality.

To establish the expected range of mean differences under Neutrality, we constructed 337 the ellipse using a Monte Carlo simulation.

Under Neutrality, participants are expected to sample from the neutral distribution, the histogram of the random generation in the control domain, meaning that random generation results in the control domain should generalise across all domains (represented by the distribution of Random generation in the left panel of Figure 3).
text.formatted: Under Neutrality, participants are expected to sample from the neutral distribution, the histogram of the random generation in the control domain, meaning that random generation results in the control domain should generalise across all domains (represented by the distribution of Random generation in the left panel of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>).

text.text: To show the plausible range of outcomes from this hypothesis, we conducted a Monte Carlo simulation, drawing samples from the neutral distribution.
The simulation was run 20,000 times, and in each iteration, 156 independent samples were drawn from the neutral distribution to match the average sequence length in Experiment 1.
This process was repeated three times, simulating the Neutrality hypothesis by maintaining a consistent distribution across all three domains.
We then calculated the mean value difference between the simulated gain and simulated control domains, and between the simulated loss and simulated control domains.

Following the central limit theorem, the joint distribution of the two types of mean value differences followed a bivariate normal distribution, of which the mean value and the covariance matrix can be estimated from the simulation results.
The 95% prediction region of this distribution is shown as an ellipse in Figure 4.
text.formatted: The 95% prediction region of this distribution is shown as an ellipse in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4</ref>.

text.text: While the previous analysis focused on the direction of participants' biases based on their mean responses, it did not consider the full response distribution.

We therefore conducted a quantitative distribution-based comparison to determine whether each participant's random generation responses were better explained by utility-independent distributions or utility-dependent distributions.
The utility-independent distribution was represented by the neutral distribution used in the visualisation analysis.
Among the utility-dependent distributions, however, only the Polarisation hypothesis can be specified quantitatively through the importance distribution defined by the UWS models.
Therefore, this comparison will focus on these two accounts.

For a single gamble, UWS assumes that people draw samples from the approximate importance distribution where o is an outcome of a gamble, p(o) is the probability of that outcome, u(o) is the utility of that outcome, ∆u(o) is the incremental gain compared with another option, and ∆u is the average utility of the outcomes in the previous similar decisions, acting like prior information.
However, there was only one option in our experiment, so ∆u(o) = u(o).
Thus, the approximate importance distribution in equation 1 simplifies to q ∝ p(o)|u(o) -u|.

(2) Lieder et al. (2018) defined the utility of an outcome o as where k was set to k = 1, o max and o min were the largest and the smallest outcome in the given choice, and ε ∼ N (0, σ) reflects neural noise.
text.formatted: (2) <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lieder et al. (2018)</ref> defined the utility of an outcome o as where k was set to k = 1, o max and o min were the largest and the smallest outcome in the given choice, and ε ∼ N (0, σ) reflects neural noise.

text.text: Since the importance distribution predicts the sampling distribution, we focused on comparing each participant's empirical histogram in the gain and loss domains with both the neutral distribution and the importance distributions.
Assuming independence among the sampled numbers, we used a multinomial likelihood function to identify the best-fitting distribution-based hypothesis for each participant across both domains.
To generate quantitative predictions from the importance distribution, several additional assumptions were required.
First, we assumed the pre-weighted distribution p(o) in equation 2 to be either the uniform or the neutral distribution.
We considered k = 1 and k = 0.5, covering the range of the utility exponent empirically identified in previous studies (e.g., Glöckner & Pachur, 2012).
text.formatted: We considered k = 1 and k = 0.5, covering the range of the utility exponent empirically identified in previous studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Glöckner & Pachur, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: When there is no prior expectation (u = 0), UWS predicts the Polarisation hypothesis.
But we also tested another version of UWS when u = u(o), representing an expectation to win or lose the average amount of money in the given gamble.
An estimate of σ ε = 0.1703, as determined by Lieder et al. (2018), was applied consistently across all the specified UWS models.
text.formatted: An estimate of σ ε = 0.1703, as determined by <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lieder et al. (2018)</ref>, was applied consistently across all the specified UWS models.

text.text: Since the utility function contains noise and the importance distribution is influenced by utilities, we ran a simulation 20,000 times to estimate the importance distribution.
In each simulation, random noise was added to each outcome's utility, and the resulting importance distribution was computed.
We then calculated the mean "importance probability" for each outcome across all simulation results.

Figure 5 presents the overlap between the empirical distributions and their best-fitted hypothetical distributions (Figure B1 displays the same figure but assuming that the pre-weighted distribution p(o) in the UWS models is the neutral distribution in Experiment 1).

text.text: Our analysis revealed that the Neutrality hypothesis outperformed the UWS models for 89% of the participants (25 out of 28, 95% CI = [71.77%, 97.73%]).
However, we identified one optimistic participant who was classified under the UWS model with k = 1, u = u(o), a model that does not predict an optimistic trend.

This discrepancy occurred because the empirical distributions overestimated "0" in the loss domain and "5" in the gain domain, whereas the importance distribution predicted an overestimation of both "0" and "5" across domains.
As a result, the importance distribution produced a higher overall likelihood than other hypotheses.
These findings suggest that, for most of the participants, the utilities of the outcomes did not influence the sampling process as predicted by the UWS models.
In this experiment, we investigated the influence of utility on the random generation task under a uniform distribution.
The group-level analysis provided substantial evidence against the utility effect.

Further individual-level analyses confirmed that the majority of the participants were unaffected by the utilities and drew samples from the same distribution, regardless of whether they were placed within the control, gain or loss The comparison between the empirical and hypothetical distributions in the gain and loss domains in Experiment 1.

domains.
These analyses did however also find a small minority of participants were seemingly influenced by utility, potentially indicating some individual differences in effects.
As a parallel measure, probability judgments were compared with the distributions produced in the random generation task.
Although the aggregate distributions showed overlap, no significant correlations were found between tasks in their distributional means or variances at the individual level.
The BFs also provided anecdotal evidence for a difference in mean responses between the two tasks.
This discrepancy may reflect the simplicity of the uniform distribution, which could have enabled participants to judge probabilities directly rather than relying on sampling.

text.text: The results of Experiment 1 supported the Neutrality hypothesis for the majority of participants when the outcomes followed a uniform distribution.
However, since most real-world lotteries have unequal probabilities, Experiment 2 employed a binomial distribution: the number of heads after flipping 10 coins.
This experiment aimed to investigate whether the Neutrality pattern observed in Experiment 1 would persist under the new scenario.
A total of 40 participants (31 women, 9 men; age: M = 23.0 years, SD = 3.7) took part in this experiment.
All participants were recruited via the University of Warwick participant pool (https://warwick.sona-systems.com/).
text.formatted: All participants were recruited via the University of Warwick participant pool (<ref type="url" target="https://warwick.sona-systems.com/">https://warwick.sona-systems.com/</ref>).

text.text: They were reimbursed with Amazon vouchers (a show-up fee of £3 and a random bonus).
The bonus was either £0 or £1, depending on the gambles at the end of the experiment.
The average payment was £3.50.
Ethical approval was given by the Humanities and Social Sciences Research Ethics Committee (HSSREC) at the University of Warwick.

The design and procedure were identical to Experiment 1 (Figure 2), with the following exceptions: participants were asked to have both the microphone and the camera on, and their video and voice were recorded.
text.formatted: The design and procedure were identical to Experiment 1 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>), with the following exceptions: participants were asked to have both the microphone and the camera on, and their video and voice were recorded.

text.text: This was only to ensure that participants remained fully attentive during the experiment.
The materials also changed.
Participants were presented with ten coins in a transparent box.
They were asked to imagine shaking the box, observing the number of heads, and responding with that number.
In the winning and losing scenarios, the number high performance standard, requiring participants to translate internal subjective impressions into explicit numerical estimates.
It can be noisy and sensitive to factors such as rounding or typing error.
Accordingly, some dispersion around the correct probabilities is expected even when participants fully understand the task instructions.
of heads represented the number of points that were won or lost, while in the control scenario, the number of heads had no meaning.
The order of the domains was counterbalanced as we did in Experiment 1, and the participants were still asked to follow a flashing dot at a pace of 37 times per minute.
In Experiment 2, participants produced a speed close to the theoretical one-an average length of 148.26 numbers (SD = 6.19) after 4 minutes.
At the end of each domain, participants received the same two questions from Experiment 1.

In the gain and loss domains, before advancing to the next block, the experimenter shook the box in front of the participants, counted the number of heads, and converted it into points (one head equals one point) that the participants won or lost (see Footnote 1).
But at the end of the control domain, the experimenter did not play this gamble.
Before the experiment ended, the experimenter calculated the total points (denoted as T).
Then the participants were given a T/20 chance to win a £1 bonus or otherwise only received the show-up fee.
The experiment took about 40 minutes to complete.

Three participants were excluded due to generating at least one sequence that was shorter than 80% of the required length (i.e., fewer than 118 numbers); one participant was excluded due to having more than three values outside of the range of 0 and 10.
The results reported below are for the final sample of 36 participants.
In the following analyses, we tested whether the predominance of Neutrality and the relationship between generation and judgment persist when probabilities are unequal.
As in Experiment 1, we initially examined participants' responses to the forced-choice question asking whether all outcomes are equally likely.

The majority of participants selected the correct answer, "unequal", across the three domains: 69% in the control domain (25 out of 36, 95% CI = [51.89%, 83.65%]), 72% in the gain domain (26 out of 36, 95% CI = [54.81%, 85.80%]), and 69% in the loss domain (25 out of 36, 95% CI = [51.89%, 83.65%]).
Table 3 provides more detailed counts.

text.text: Furthermore, we conducted a comparison of the proportion of "unequal" responses in the gain and loss domains relative to the control domain.

Using McNemar's test with continuity correction, we are still unable to reject the null hypothesis, which states that participants report the same pattern of probability based on our manipulation of the gain or loss domain.
Specifically, the test results were χ 2 (1, N = 36) = 0, p = 1.0 for the control-gain comparison and χ 2 (1, N = 36) = 0, p = 1.0 for the control-loss comparison, after a Holm-Bonferroni correction.

To evaluate the consistency between probability judgment and the histogram of the random generation, we compared them with each other and assessed both against the binomial distribution using one-sample t tests (Figure 6).

Notably, both the probability judgments and the distributions of random generation exhibited a significant departure from the expected binomial distribution, reflecting a "flattened" shape consistent with prior research showing that participants produce sampling distributions that are flatter than the true probabilities (Peterson et al., 1968; Teigen, 1974).

text.text: The overlapping index was also employed to examine the similarity between these two distributions: Their values were all equal to or higher than 75%, indicating a high level of similarity between the explicit probability judgments and random generation relative frequencies.
At the individual level, we analysed the correlation of the mean values and of the variance between the random generation histogram and probability judgment, shown in Table 4.

text.text: We found that the correlations of the mean values were significant in all three domains, and the correlation of the variance was also significant in the loss domain, meaning participants' random generations and probability judgments are strongly related.
The consistency between these tasks reinforces the idea that random generation can provide valuable insights into how people intuitively evaluate probabilities.
To examine whether introducing unequal outcome probabilities changed our conclusion about utility sensitivity, we first tested whether random generation differed across domains.
Similar to Experiment 1, participants tended to generate the lowest values in the loss domain (M loss = 4.66), followed by the control domain (M control = 4.98), and the gain domain (M gain = 5.02).
However, the RM-BANOVA with domain as the factor provided substantial evidence against the domain effect (BF = 1/9.43).
As a secondary comparison, probability judgments showed a similar descriptive pattern: The means from lowest to highest are M loss = 4.91, M control = 5.08, and M gain = 5.12.
We next compared the means of probability judgments and of random generation using an RM-BANOVA with domain, task and their interaction as factors.
The BF for domains, tasks and their interactions are 1/1.92, 1.63, and 1/3.97, respectively.
We next explored the individual differences in the effect of the domains.
Following the same analytical framework as in Experiment 1, we first applied an RM-BANOVA to assess whether each participant showed evidence of a domain effect.
We then visualised the direction of each participant's responses to identify which hypothesis they were consistent with.
Finally, we compared each participant's response distribution with the predictions of the Neutrality hypothesis and the UWS models.
Individual RM-BANOVA.
The individual analyses again favoured Neutrality for most participants.
As shown in Table A2, 69% of participants (25 out of 36, 95% CI = [51.89%, 83.65%]) had a BF below 1/3, revealing that the majority remained unaffected by the domains.

text.text: Following Experiment 1, the region of the Neutrality hypothesis was estimated through Monte Carlo simulation, using 146 independent samples per simulated sequence to match the average sequence length in Experiment 2.

Overall, 72% of the participants (26 out of 36, 95% CI = [54.81%, 85.80%]) fell within the ellipse, while five participants were in the Centralisation region, two in the Polarisation region, and three in the Optimism region.

One participant with a BF of the domains below 1/3 fell outside the Neutrality ellipse, because the participant's personal neutral distribution deviated from the neutral distribution used to estimate the Neutrality ellipse.
Thus, this discrepancy does not necessarily indicate sensitivity to domain.
The distribution-based comparison provided converging evidence.

Using the same distribution-based likelihood comparison as in Experiment 1, but with the binomial distribution as the pre-weighted distribution p(o) for the UWS models, the Neutrality hypothesis was still the best model for 78% of the participants (28 out of 36, 95% CI = [60.85%, 89.88%]).  domain effects and the fit to participants' generation distributions.

Experiment 2 extends the Neutrality pattern observed in Experiment 1 to binomial distributions.

Even when using outcomes with unequal probabilities, our results continue to demonstrate that for most individuals, the utility did not influence the sampling patterns, though again there is some indication of heterogeneity in this effect.
On the other hand, probabilities did influence the sampling proportions, with the higher probability head counts being more often randomly generated.

Moreover, our observations align with prior research showing flatter subjective distributions in controlled statistical scenarios (Peterson et al., 1968; Teigen, 1974) and in more naturalistic settings (Castillo et al., 2026; León-Villagrá et al., 2026).

text.text: One could argue that this flattening is qualitatively consistent with oversampling rare outcomes, as illustrated in Figure When comparing probability judgments with random generation, we found high overlapping indices and a significant positive correlation between their mean values, although the BF provided anecdotal evidence against the indifference between tasks.
These findings suggest that when the distribution becomes harder to derive, participants may rely more heavily on the sampling process to guide their probability judgments.
Experiments 1 and 2 demonstrated a consistent Neutrality pattern at both the group level and individual level: Most participants remained unbiased by utilities under the random generation paradigm.
This contrasts with the well-documented desirability bias typically observed with the Marks paradigm (Krizan & Windschitl, 2007).
text.formatted: This contrasts with the well-documented desirability bias typically observed with the Marks paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Krizan & Windschitl, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: To explore the source of this discrepancy, Experiment 3 was designed to compare our approach with the Marks paradigm from an experimental design perspective.
First, the Marks paradigm employs a card-drawing scenario rather than raffles or coin tosses, so we adopted the same card-drawing scenario for the random generation task in Experiment 3.
However, it also differs in the number of possible outcomes.
Whereas the Marks paradigm typically involves dichotomous outcomes, Experiments 1 and 2 used scenarios with up to 11 outcomes.
To examine whether the number of outcomes influences sampling behaviour, Experiment 3 compared gambles with two outcomes and with six outcomes.
A second difference lies in the task instructions: participants were asked to imagine drawing a card in the random generation task and to predict which card would be drawn in the Marks paradigm.
To capture both approaches, Experiment 3 incorporated both types of instructions.

Another methodological difference is the level of repetition: the Marks paradigm requires participants to give only a single response, whereas the random generation paradigm involves repeated responses.
Experiment 3 addressed this difference by manipulating the level of repetition.

In summary, Experiment 3 built on the domain manipulations in Experiments 1 and 2 while introducing three additional independent variables for comparison with the Marks paradigm: task instruction (random generation or prediction), repetition (one-off task or a task repeated 10 times), and number of outcomes (two or six).
By systematically varying these factors, we aimed to identify which elements of the design might cause discrepancies in the influence of utility.
A total of 154 participants (132 women, 20 men, 2 other; age: M = 18.7 years, SD = 0.8) were recruited via the University of Warwick's subject pool.
Participants received course credit for taking part, and no monetary incentives were offered due to platform restrictions.
Ethical approval was given by the Humanities and Social Sciences Research Ethics Committee (HSSREC) at the University of Warwick.
Experiment 3 employed a within-subjects design with 24 different conditions (3 domains × 2 tasks × 2 levels of repetition × 2 levels of number of outcomes).
To maintain task consistency, participants either began with prediction tasks followed by random generation tasks or started with random generation tasks followed by prediction tasks.
After each task, a comprehension check question would appear: "Which task have you been asked to do?"
with two options provided: "imagine drawing cards" and "predict cards to be drawn".
Within each task, a Latin square design was used to balance the order of the 12 conditions (3 domains × 2 levels of repetition × 2 levels of number of outcomes).

This approach created 24 possible condition orders, and we ensured that the number of participants assigned to each order was as balanced as possible, with the difference in sample size across orders kept to no more than one.
Participants were shown a figure of six cards.

In the two-outcome condition, three cards were labelled "0" and three were labelled "5" in the control domain; three were labelled "+0" and three "+5" in the gain domain; and three were labelled "-0" and three "-5" in the loss domain.
In the six-outcome condition, the cards were labelled with numbers ranging from "0" to "5" in the control domain, "+0" to "+5" in the gain domain, and "-0" to "-5" in the loss domain.
The experimental program was developed using PsychoPy3 (version 2023.2.3; Peirce et al., 2019) and conducted online.
Figure 9 illustrates the procedure for a condition in Experiment 3.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">9</ref> illustrates the procedure for a condition in Experiment 3.

text.text: At the start of each condition, participants were introduced to the gamble, where the cards would be shuffled, and a random card drawn with replacement.
In the random generation task, participants were instructed to imagine drawing a card, while in the prediction task, participants were asked to predict the value on a randomly drawn card.
The full text of the instructions for each condition is included in Appendix C.
After the instruction screen, participants had 30 seconds to enter their imagined or predicted value in a text box and click the "Next" button to continue.
To ensure participants maintained awareness of the domain, they had to include the symbols "+" and "-" with each input in the gain and loss domains to proceed.
If no input was provided within 30 seconds, the program advanced automatically.

Once a response had been submitted, the program executed the gamble, displayed an animation of the cards being shuffled and drawn, and recorded the outcome without revealing it immediately to the participant.

Although no monetary rewards were used, participants were given 220 points at the beginning of the experiment to establish a context of winning and losing, and they viewed their aggregated results at the end.
