Three criteria were used for data exclusion, and participants meeting any of these were excluded: First, participants with more than 13 invalid inputs (10% out of the 132 inputs in total) across the experiment were excluded (n = 3); 3 Second, participants who failed both comprehension checks regarding the task instructions were excluded (n = 4); Third, we excluded participants whose random sequences were extremely predictable in any of the four repeated-control conditions (prediction vs. random generation and two-vs.
six-outcome; n = 52).
4 Taking all three criteria together, the final sample comprised 98 participants.

The third criterion was assessed using "determinism" (DET), which measures the proportion of recurrent subsequences within a sequence (Marwan et al., 2007, see Appendix 3 Invalid inputs were defined as those that were not possible (e.g., number "6") or were missing responses.

subsequences.
For example, the sequence {5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0} yields a DET of 92%.
DET has previously been used as an exclusion criterion in random generation studies (e.g., Castillo et al., 2024).
text.formatted: DET has previously been used as an exclusion criterion in random generation studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Castillo et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We applied it to both random generation and prediction tasks because both required repeated responses to independently drawn outcomes, allowing us to assess sequential regularity across tasks.
To avoid domain effects, we applied this measure only to sequences in the control condition, setting the exclusion threshold to 90% (see Appendix D for the rationale behind this threshold).
Such highly predictable sequences may reflect reliance on simplified response rules rather than considering each draw separately.
To assess whether our conclusions were sensitive to this criterion, we also re-ran the analyses without applying the DET criterion; these supplementary results are reported in Appendix F.

Having established the final sample and clarified the exclusion criteria, we now turn to the main research questions: whether the influence of outcome utility on participants' responses varies with task instructions, repetition, or outcome structure.
First, we illustrated how the numbers were distributed in the two-and six-outcome conditions, as shown in Figure 10.

text.text: For each participant, we calculated the frequency of each number across the levels of domains and numbers of outcomes.

text.text: Overall, the results provided evidence for main effects of repetition and domain, as well as for their interaction, but evidence against effects of task, number of outcomes, or any other interactions.
However, the lack of an effect of task instruction may reflect a failed manipulation.
Participants could reasonably have interpreted the two instructions as equivalent.
To examine this possibility, we re-analysed only the first block using a one-way Bayesian ANOVA with task treated as a between-subjects factor.
This allowed us to compare participants' responses before they had encountered both sets of instructions.
The analysis yielded a BF of 1/21.32, providing strong evidence that task instruction did not influence the mental sampling results.

Although the group-level analysis revealed an optimistic bias, this finding does not 703 establish whether optimism characterised most participants or was driven by a smaller 704 subset of individuals.

We first applied an RM-BANOVA to each participant's data to 705 assess the effects we found in the group-level analysis; we then visualised the extent to 706 which each participant's responses aligned with the proposed hypotheses, before comparing 707 their complete response distributions with the predictions of the Neutrality hypothesis and 708 the UWS models.

Together, these analyses allowed us to unmask substantial individual 709 heterogeneity, identify the direction of any utility-related biases, and determine which 710 theoretical account best explained each participant's mental sampling.
Individual RM-BANOVA.
The group-level analysis identified three influential factors: domain, repetition, and their interaction.
To examine whether these effects also held at the individual level, we conducted an RM-BANOVA for each participant, including domain, repetition, and their interaction as factors.
For this analysis, each participant's data were divided into six cells, containing either 4 or 40 trials per cell.

text.text: The results indicate that the majority of participants were unaffected by the variables: 78% for the domains (76 out of 98, CI = [68.01%, 85.36%]), 70% for the repetition (69 out of 98, 95% CI = [60.34%, 79.21%]), and 84% for their interaction (82 out of 98, 95% CI = [74.84%, 90.37%]).
Next, we analysed the two-and six-outcome conditions separately to examine whether utility insensitivity was a participant-specific tendency that generalises across outcome structures.
Each participant's responses were split by outcome condition, yielding 66 responses per subset.
For each subset, the domain effect was then tested with an RM-BANOVA.
If the domain effect is consistent across different numbers of outcomes, the BFs for the two-and six-outcome conditions should be positively correlated.
This was indeed the case (Pearson correlation coefficient after Box-Cox transformation: r(96) = .54, p < .001).

text.text: These findings confirm the robustness of the individual-level BFs.
To provide a more independent test of whether utility insensitivity generalised across outcome structures, we also conducted a cross-condition validation analysis.
We classified participants according to their individual BFs in one outcome structure and tested whether this classification predicted their responses in the other.
Although the classifications may not be perfect, systematic individual differences should still produce distinct domain effects across subgroups.
As we expected, both directions of validation provided evidence for an interaction between domain and subgroup categorisation (BFs = 19.12 and 2.86 × 10 9 , respectively).

Distribution evaluation.
The distribution evaluation provides insights into whether complete sampling distributions favour Neutrality or the UWS predictions.
The same method was used to calculate the importance distributions of the UWS models; the pre-weighted distribution p(o) was the two-and six-outcome uniform distributions, respectively.
For each participant, the likelihood of each hypothesis was evaluated and summed across the four empirical distributions (gain vs. loss and two vs. six outcomes).

As shown in Figure 13 (Figure B3 displays the same figure but assuming that the pre-weighted distribution p(o) in the UWS models is the neutral distribution in Experiment 3), we found 83% of the participants (82 out of 98, 95% CI = [74.84%, 90.37%]) were best fitted by the Neutrality hypothesis.

In Experiment 3, we investigated whether differences in experimental design could explain the discrepancy between our earlier findings favouring Neutrality and the optimistic bias reported using the Marks paradigm.
By manipulating the task instruction, the number of outcomes and the repetition of the tasks, we replicated the Marks paradigm while directly comparing it with the random generation task.
At the group-level analysis, we observed the Optimism bias, consistent with previous findings using the Marks paradigm (Irwin, 1953; Krizan & Windschitl, 2007; Marks, 1951).
text.formatted: At the group-level analysis, we observed the Optimism bias, consistent with previous findings using the Marks paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Irwin, 1953;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Krizan & Windschitl, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Marks, 1951)</ref>.

text.text: For the manipulation of the experimental design, we found that participants were not influenced by task instruction or the number of outcomes, but were affected by repetition.
However, the individual-level analysis revealed substantial heterogeneity, with more than half of the participants uninfluenced by repetition or domains.
These results highlight the presence of an unbiased majority and emphasise the importance of individual-level analysis, as group-level analyses alone may obscure distinct patterns of mental sampling.

To address these concerns, Experiment 4 introduced larger, tangible monetary incentives in a laboratory setting, offering a stronger test of whether utility affects mental simulation when outcome magnitudes are more pronounced.
Another issue concerns the prediction task in Experiment 3.

In similar studies, participants are often rewarded for accuracy (e.g., Budescu & Bruderman, 1995; Crandall et al., 1955) or receive feedback, such as being shown the actual results after making their predictions (e.g., Park et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In similar studies, participants are often rewarded for accuracy (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Budescu & Bruderman, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Crandall et al., 1955)</ref> or receive feedback, such as being shown the actual results after making their predictions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Park et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In our study, however, the bonus had to remain independent of participants' responses, as it was designed only to embed outcomes within a meaningful gain-loss context, rather than to reward accuracy.

This approach ensured that participants experienced outcomes as wins or losses while allowing us to examine how such utilities influence mental simulation, without introducing strategic incentives that could bias responding.
To address this, Experiment 4 provided feedback on their accuracy after each condition, a feature not included in Experiment 3.
This adjustment aimed to make the task more comparable to other prediction tasks in the literature.

With Experiment 4, we explored whether the results found in Experiment 3 are robust after we increase the magnitude of the incentive and the distinction between the random generation and the prediction tasks.

text.text: Additionally, card values represented monetary values rather than points, indicated by adding a pound sign (£) in front of the numbers for the gain and loss domain.
This change aimed to make the concept of utility more concrete and to allow incentivization with larger monetary incentives compared to Experiments 1 and 2.
Similar to Experiment 3, the program played the gambles after each condition and saved the results.
At the end of the experiment, one result from each type of gamble (gains vs. losses and two vs. six outcomes) was randomly selected and summed to determine the bonus.
Since all outcomes were based on chance, the actual bonus depended on the randomly selected results.
As we used the same gambles in Experiment 3, the worst possible result was losing £10.
The participants were initially given a cash note of £10, which was put in front of them throughout the experiment and could gain or lose from it depending on the results of the gambles.
The experimental program was also modified in a few ways.

In the prediction task, participants received feedback on their accuracy and the average accuracy (50% in the two-outcome condition and 17% in the six-outcome condition) after each condition, whereas no feedback was provided in the random generation task.
The second change involved adding a comprehension check after presenting the information sheet.
This check asked whether the bonus amount depended on participants' responses or was unrelated:
Participants who answered incorrectly had to reread the information sheet and attempt the question again.
Notably, performance on this comprehension check was not part of the exclusion criteria.
As we preregistered, we excluded participants who had more than 13 invalid inputs (n = 1) or failed both comprehension checks (n = 3), leaving a sample of 44 participants.
We also preregistered an exclusion criterion based on DET, whereby participants with DET exceeding 90% in any of the repeated-control conditions would be excluded.
However, 31 participants met this criterion, and excluding these participants would have removed the majority of the sample, leaving insufficient data for meaningful analysis.

The following analyses therefore omitted this criterion, though for transparency, we report analyses using the originally planned exclusion criteria in Appendix G, which yielded a sample size of 15 participants.
These results are largely consistent with those obtained using the sample of 44 participants.

In Experiment 4, we increased the salience of the monetary context and made the distinction between the random generation task and the prediction task more pronounced.
At the group level, we found decisive evidence that people were influenced by the domains.
We also found strong or very strong evidence against the effects of the task, number of outcomes and repetition.

Further individual-level analyses revealed a clear shift from Experiment 3 to Experiment 4: whereas most participants were not influenced by domain in Experiment 3, the majority were influenced in Experiment 4.

This domain effect was consistent across both two-outcome and six-outcome gambles, suggesting that utility-based biases became more prevalent when the incentives associated with the gambles were more salient.

In the quantitative analysis of individuals' biases, we found that the number of participants falling within the Neutrality ellipses and the Optimism region was nearly equal for both the two-outcome and six-outcome conditions.

We investigated the impact of the utility of outcomes on mental simulations in 966 various gambles with descriptive probabilities.
Experiments 1 and 2 showed consistent 967 support for the Neutrality hypothesis at both the group and individual levels, indicating that mental simulation was largely unaffected by utility.
In Experiment 3, the group-level analysis supported the Optimism hypothesis, suggesting a tendency to simulate outcomes with higher utility.

One possible explanation for this difference is the smaller number of repetitions: within Experiment 3, optimistic sampling was more pronounced for the one-off condition, whereas responses became neutral as more outcomes were generated.
However, because the experiments also differed in outcome structure and other procedural features, these factors cannot be fully disentangled.
Individual-level results further revealed considerable heterogeneity, with more than half of the participants unbiased by utilities, aligning with the Neutrality hypothesis.
Experiment 4 identified a shift of this pattern:
When the monetary context of the gambles became more salient, fewer than half of the participants remained unbiased, while most of the biased participants exhibited an Optimism bias.

In the visualisation of individual biases, several data points outside the ellipse lay close to the ordinate axis (see Figures 12 and 16), indicating that a few participants produced similar mean values in the control and gain conditions.

text.text: This pattern suggests that the similarity we observed is unlikely to reflect a misunderstanding of the task.
A more plausible explanation is that people tend to interpret plain numbers as implicit "gains", even when the materials in the control and gain conditions differ substantially, as in Experiment 4.
Further research should examine this tendency more systematically.

Quantitatively, we compared the Neutrality hypothesis with four different versions of the importance distributions defined in the UWS models, two of which provide a quantitative description of the Polarisation hypothesis.
Our findings revealed that the Neutrality hypothesis emerged as the winning model across all experiments-although it was not as dominant in Experiment 4 as it had been in the first three experiments.
However, we also observed that some optimistic individuals were classified under the U-shaped importance distribution in Experiments 1, 3, and 4.
This occurred because the U-shaped distributions were the only available forms capable of capturing the pattern of oversampling better gains and undersampling worse losses.
These results suggest that the underlying sampling process does not align with the mechanisms described by the UWS model.

Moreover, the apparent dominance of the Neutrality hypothesis may partly reflect the absence of a quantitative "optimistic distribution", highlighting the need to formalise such distributions for future modelling work.
Next, we consider several factors that may have influenced the results.
One important factor is the level of monetary contexts across experiments.
In Experiments 1 and 2, which offered small rewards, no group-level effects of utility were observed.
In contrast, Experiment 3, which provided no real monetary incentives but only symbolic "points", nevertheless produced a clear optimism bias at the group level (see also, Irwin, 1953; Marks, 1951).
text.formatted: In contrast, Experiment 3, which provided no real monetary incentives but only symbolic "points", nevertheless produced a clear optimism bias at the group level (see also, <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Irwin, 1953;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Marks, 1951)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that the presence or absence of utility effects cannot be explained solely by the size of the incentives.
However, stronger incentives may enhance motivational engagement and amplify utility-based biases, as observed in Experiment 4.
Future studies should systematically manipulate the salience of real payoffs to clarify how monetary incentives shape optimism and neutrality in mental simulation.
Another concern is the asymmetry between the control condition and the gain or loss conditions.
Across all four experiments, responses in the control condition were shorter than those in the other two.
This means that the domain manipulation involved not only outcome valence but also differences in responses such as linguistic load and format.
However, this difference does not undermine our main conclusions.
The design ensured that the control condition lacked utility information, which was the key aspect we intended to isolate.
Our central comparisons focus on the gain and loss domains, using the control as a neutral baseline rather than a direct contrast.
Therefore, even if the control condition differed in presentation length, the observed effects of utility remain valid because the gain and loss domains were symmetrically manipulated.

Future studies could nonetheless improve upon this design by matching the linguistic format across domains, for example by adding neutral verbal markers such as "number 5" or "#5", to isolate the influence of responses more precisely.
A third consideration concerns why more participants showed optimism in Experiment 4.
We attributed this pattern to the increased monetary incentives, consistent with earlier findings (e.g., Crandall et al., 1955).
text.formatted: We attributed this pattern to the increased monetary incentives, consistent with earlier findings (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Crandall et al., 1955)</ref>.

text.text: An alternative explanation is that some participants may have believed their responses could influence the outcome.
To minimise this possibility, we have included a comprehension check explicitly stating that their answers would not affect their bonus.
Moreover, previous research has found that the illusion of control plays a limited role in such tasks (see Krizan & Windschitl, 2007, p.103, for a review).
text.formatted: Moreover, previous research has found that the illusion of control plays a limited role in such tasks (see <ref type="bibr">Krizan & Windschitl, 2007, p.103,</ref> for a review).

text.text: Nevertheless, it remains possible that some participants distrusted the In addition to our main findings, exploratory analyses (see Appendix H) revealed that participants often showed systematic tendencies in how they initiated simulations.
The direction of this starting-point bias varied across experiments, sometimes favouring lower values, more probable values, or more desirable outcomes.
Although inconsistent, these results suggest that the initiation of mental simulation may itself be influenced by factors beyond probability and utility, and warrant further investigation.
We compared the results of probability judgment and random generation tasks in Experiments 1 and 2, as well as the results of prediction and random generation tasks in Experiments 3 and 4.
These comparisons reveal many similarities between the tasks.

First, the findings from Experiments 1 and 2 show that probability judgments and histograms of random generation are similar to each other, particularly when the specific probabilities are hard to derive, such as binomial distributions (Experiment 2).
However, in simpler contexts, participants may bypass simulation and instead estimate probabilities directly using descriptive statistics or common knowledge.
Second, the results of Experiments 3 and 4 indicate that the prediction tasks produced outcomes similar to the random generation tasks, especially in the absence of accuracy feedback.

The similarity across tasks suggests that mental simulation, as assumed by many sampling models (e.g., Costello & Watts, 2014 , 2016; Zhu et al., 2020), could offer a plausible and unifying account of certain findings in prediction and probability judgments, particularly related to the desirability bias (referred to as the Optimism hypothesis in our study).

text.text: For instance, Park et al. (2022) reported that predictions show a much stronger desirability bias, which they attributed to the influence of non-normative factors, such as hunches.

text.text: There is a potential alternative explanation: The prediction may be based on fewer samples than the likelihood judgments (as also suggested by Sundh et al., 2023), leading to a stronger Optimism effect observed in predictions compared to likelihood judgments.

text.text: In addition, as reviewed by Krizan and Windschitl (2007), the effect of the desirability bias is strongest when the two outcomes of a gamble have equal probabilities (50/50), but is weaker when the probabilities are unequal.

text.text: Although our study did not explicitly test the interaction between probability and utility in the one-off condition, the influence of probabilities on the repeated mental simulations that we found in Experiment 2 suggests that participants prioritised probability over utility.
We speculate that this tendency extends to the one-off condition, reflecting a cognitive heuristic that favours probability more than utility.
Although we find similarities across these tasks, the present experiments cannot directly determine the causal link between them.
Explicit generation is not necessarily identical to the implicit evidence considered when making predictions or probability judgments.
In simple scenarios, people may rely on non-sampling mechanisms, as may have occurred in the probability judgment task in Experiment 1.
In addition, the evidence people rely on may not always take the form of a sequence of outcomes.

In some cases, judgments may instead depend on other features of the event, such as when predicting the result of an election (e.g., Todorov et al., 2005) or a sport event (e.g., Pachur & Biele, 2007).
text.formatted: In some cases, judgments may instead depend on other features of the event, such as when predicting the result of an election (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Todorov et al., 2005)</ref> or a sport event (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Pachur & Biele, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: One way to test the causal link in future work would be to examine whether interfering with the sampling process disrupts probability judgments.
We therefore treat random generation as a process-level measure that suggests the sequence and distribution of outcomes generated during the mental simulation of a gamble-like event.

Previous research has primarily focused on participants' probability estimates for binary events (e.g., Costello & Watts, 2014 , 2016; Zhu et al., 2020), or on predictions of a single outcome (Crandall et al., 1955; Irwin, 1953; Marks, 1951).
text.formatted: Previous research has primarily focused on participants' probability estimates for binary events (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Costello & Watts, 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Zhu et al., 2020)</ref>, or on predictions of a single outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Crandall et al., 1955;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Irwin, 1953;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Marks, 1951)</ref>.

text.text: These responses compress the participant's representation of the event into one aggregate value.
By contrast, the random generation task indicates the content of the mental simulation that can inform probability judgment and prediction.
Consistent with this interpretation, Spicer et al. (2026) applied the random generation paradigm to risky choices and examined whether generated sequences predicted participants' choices.
text.formatted: Consistent with this interpretation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Spicer et al. (2026)</ref> applied the random generation paradigm to risky choices and examined whether generated sequences predicted participants' choices.

text.text: They found that the average utility of the generated sequences reliably predicted choice even after accounting for the expected utility of the gambles, suggesting that random generation can provide process-relevant information about the representations underlying subsequent decisions.

Interestingly, Spicer et al. (2026) also did not find evidence of a value bias in generations, though unlike the present paper they did not directly contrast the same distribution in differing domains.
text.formatted: Interestingly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Spicer et al. (2026)</ref> also did not find evidence of a value bias in generations, though unlike the present paper they did not directly contrast the same distribution in differing domains.

text.text: Additionally, Spicer et al.
(2026) did not perform the individual-level classification to bias hypotheses used here so the possibility of individual differences in bias in their data remains.
Our study highlights the importance of considering individual differences in psychological research.
First, group-level analyses can reveal the influence of an experimental manipulation on average, but they cannot determine how widely that influence is shared across individuals.
Even sophisticated statistical approaches, such as the mixed-effects models used in our group-level analysis, may fail to fully account for the diversity of individual responses.
For instance, the group-level analysis of Experiment 3 suggested the effect of domains.
However, our individual-level analyses showed that this effect was driven by a subset of participants exhibiting a substantial shift, rather than by a small shift shared across the entire sample.
This finding illustrates how individual-level analyses can reveal meaningful subgroups that remain obscured when behaviour is examined only at the group level (Frankot et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This finding illustrates how individual-level analyses can reveal meaningful subgroups that remain obscured when behaviour is examined only at the group level <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Frankot et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Individual-level analyses are also valuable when the group-level analysis shows a null effect.
As noted by Kievit et al. (2013), a null result at the group level may arise because subgroups exhibit effects in opposite directions that cancel each other when averaged.
text.formatted: As noted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Kievit et al. (2013)</ref>, a null result at the group level may arise because subgroups exhibit effects in opposite directions that cancel each other when averaged.

text.text: Individual-level analyses help distinguish this possibility from a genuine absence of an effect.
In the present study, participants could exhibit one of four distinct patterns of bias, making such cancellation possible.
Consequently, even after Experiments 1 and 2 provided evidence supporting the Neutrality hypothesis at the group level, we continued to examine the influence of the domains for each participant.
This approach enabled us to distinguish genuine neutrality from heterogeneous patterns of opposing biases.
Apart from their statistical value, individual-level analyses may also provide valuable psychological insights.
In Experiments 3 and 4, we identified two behavioural patterns, Neutrality and Optimism.

Although the present study was not designed to explain the origins of this heterogeneity, previous research suggests that individual variation in risky judgment and decision making may reflect differences in the use of cognitive heuristics (e.g., Shaham et al., 1992), cognitive abilities (e.g., Peters et al., 2006) or personality (e.g., Huang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Although the present study was not designed to explain the origins of this heterogeneity, previous research suggests that individual variation in risky judgment and decision making may reflect differences in the use of cognitive heuristics (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Shaham et al., 1992)</ref>, cognitive abilities (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Peters et al., 2006)</ref> or personality (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Huang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Future research could investigate whether these factors account for the behavioural patterns observed here, thereby providing a deeper understanding of the cognitive mechanisms underlying utility's influence on random generation.

Our findings have theoretical implications for sampling-based models of cognitive processes involved in evaluating risky events, such as probability judgments (e.g., Zhu et al., 2020 Zhu et al., , 2024)), which assume people generate samples from an internal distribution of possible outcomes.
text.formatted: Our findings have theoretical implications for sampling-based models of cognitive processes involved in evaluating risky events, such as probability judgments (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Zhu et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Zhu et al., , 2024))</ref>, which assume people generate samples from an internal distribution of possible outcomes.

text.text: They can also extend to models of risky choices (e.g., Bhatia, 2014; Busemeyer & Diederich, 2002; Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993; Lieder et al., 2018), which characterise decision-making as a process of comparing options through sequences of sampled outcomes.
text.formatted: They can also extend to models of risky choices (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bhatia, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Busemeyer & Diederich, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lieder et al., 2018)</ref>, which characterise decision-making as a process of comparing options through sequences of sampled outcomes.

text.text: In broad terms, these models can be grouped into three categories according to the distributions from which samples are drawn: (1) sampling that strictly follows the objective probability distribution; (2) sampling from a distorted version of the objective distribution that is independent of utilities; and (3) sampling from a distribution that depends on utility.
Across four experiments, we tested a prominent instantiation of the third category, the UWS model, which predicts oversampling of the best gains and the worst losses.
We evaluated this account by comparing participants' empirical random generation distributions with the importance distributions implied by UWS.
Overall, the data did not support the central UWS prediction.
Instead, most participants showed either neutrality or optimism, with the balance between these patterns varying with the salience of the monetary context and with individual differences.

Our data also provide evidence towards the second category of models: in Experiment 2, where the outcomes were not equally likely, participants' empirical generation distributions were flatter than the corresponding objective distributions, even in the control condition.
This finding suggests a tendency to overestimate small proportions and underestimate large proportions, indicating that such biases do not necessarily arise from outcome utility.

This pattern echoes earlier work investigating people's subjective probability distributions (Hollands & Dyre, 2000; Peterson et al., 1968), and particularly resembles the predictions of distracted decision field theory (see p. 1099, in Bhatia, 2014), a model that introduces stochastic error in sampling to account for a range of behavioural paradoxes in risky choice.
text.formatted: This pattern echoes earlier work investigating people's subjective probability distributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hollands & Dyre, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Peterson et al., 1968)</ref>, and particularly resembles the predictions of distracted decision field theory (see p. 1099, in Bhatia, 2014), a model that introduces stochastic error in sampling to account for a range of behavioural paradoxes in risky choice.

text.text: Taken together, our results suggest that models of decision making should allow for deviations from objective probability that arise both with and without utility.

More importantly, the substantial individual heterogeneity observed across our experiments suggests a potential mixture account of mental sampling: Some individuals remain insensitive to outcome utilities, whereas others show an optimistic bias that over-represents favourable outcomes.
The relative prevalence of these response patterns also varied across experimental contexts, with optimistic responses becoming more prevalent when monetary outcomes were more salient.
These findings highlight the importance of accounting for both the coexistence of distinct sampling tendencies and their variation across contexts.
Future models should therefore accommodate individual differences in how outcome utility influences mental sampling, rather than assuming a uniform sampling process across individuals.

One possible criticism of this interpretation is that the current experiments did not offer sufficiently extreme outcomes as in the Russian roulette example, which originally motivated the UWS model (Lieder et al., 2018).
text.formatted: One possible criticism of this interpretation is that the current experiments did not offer sufficiently extreme outcomes as in the Russian roulette example, which originally motivated the UWS model <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Lieder et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A direct experimental analogue is difficult to construct because the defining feature of Russian roulette is a rare but catastrophic outcome.

Experiment 4 introduced real monetary consequences, with losses of up to £10, but such bounded monetary losses cannot reproduce the consequences associated with death or similarly catastrophic outcomes.

The present experiments therefore allow us to examine whether utility influences sampling under meaningful monetary stakes, but not whether the sampling process changes qualitatively when a rare outcome has catastrophic consequences.

A possibility raised by the Russian roulette example is a constrained form of Neutrality in which sampling remains broadly probability-based but the decision maker ensures that the rare disaster is considered, for example by starting the simulation with the worst outcome.

However, our starting-point analysis (Appendix H) does not support this suggestion: participants instead tended to start from relatively smaller absolute values, even when monetary loss was salient in Experiment 4.
There is thus little evidence of such a starting rule in these data, though further examination of the time course of generation may be valuable.
More fundamentally, avoiding Russian roulette does not necessarily require the catastrophic outcome to appear first, or even to be over-sampled.
The present experiments examine how outcomes are generated, but not how those samples are subsequently evaluated and translated into choice.
For example, once a generated sequence contains at least one catastrophic outcome, a minimax heuristic (Coombs et al., 1970, Chapter 5) could be sufficient to lead to rejection of the gamble.
text.formatted: For example, once a generated sequence contains at least one catastrophic outcome, a minimax heuristic <ref type="bibr">(Coombs et al., 1970, Chapter 5</ref>) could be sufficient to lead to rejection of the gamble.

text.text: Even if a short sequence contained only survival outcomes, the decision maker could still retain a strong prior belief that death is possible and reject the gamble without relying exclusively on the sampled sequence.
Thus, the Russian roulette case highlights the need to distinguish the generation of outcome samples from the evaluation of those samples and their translation into final decisions.
This study examined how utility influences the perception of probability in a sample of university students in England.
Our tasks required participants to understand fundamental concepts such as probability, random generation, and prediction, which rely on basic numeracy skills.
Research indicates that numeracy skills vary with educational exposure, age, and cultural background (Klaczynski et al., 2019; Peters et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Research indicates that numeracy skills vary with educational exposure, age, and cultural background <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Klaczynski et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Peters et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the proportion of biased versus unbiased individuals observed in our study may not generalise to all age, educational levels or cultural contexts.
However, our individual-level analyses provide a useful framework for exploring these individual differences across diverse educational backgrounds and cultures.
Furthermore, our study focused exclusively on how participants simulate gambles based on descriptive information.

Since prior research has shown that people behave differently when making decisions from description versus experience (Hertwig & Erev, 2009), it is reasonable to infer that simulation processes may also differ when based on experiential information.
text.formatted: Since prior research has shown that people behave differently when making decisions from description versus experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hertwig & Erev, 2009)</ref>, it is reasonable to infer that simulation processes may also differ when based on experiential information.

text.text: Several studies have explored how utility influences experience or memory.
For example, the extreme gains and losses are often overestimated during the memory encoding process (Madan et al., 2021), though these studies did not examine the time course of these effects.
text.formatted: For example, the extreme gains and losses are often overestimated during the memory encoding process <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Madan et al., 2021)</ref>, though these studies did not examine the time course of these effects.

text.text: On the other hand, Szollosi et al. (2023) asked participants to generate sequences of outcomes a gamble might provide if the experiment continued.
text.formatted: On the other hand, <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Szollosi et al. (2023)</ref> asked participants to generate sequences of outcomes a gamble might provide if the experiment continued.

text.text: However, they did not evaluate the probabilities of different outcomes within those sequences.
Applying the random generation paradigm to gambles based on experience could therefore provide valuable insights into the interaction between memory and utility over time.
In conclusion, utility's influence reveals important heterogeneity in mental simulation processes.
Across four experiments, mental simulations often remained uninfluenced by outcome domain, consistent with the Neutrality hypothesis.

At the same time, a reliable subgroup showed an Optimism bias, over-sampling favourable outcomes and under-sampling unfavourable ones, with this tendency becoming more prevalent when the monetary context was made more salient.
We also found evidence suggesting that random generation is related to probability judgments and predictions.

Based on these findings, we recommend that both empirical studies and theoretical models in this field account for individual differences in the influence of utility on simulation processes, particularly the coexistence of largely unbiased sampling and optimistic, utility-sensitive sampling.

These findings indicate that the response in the one-off condition should not be treated as equivalent to the starting point of a sequence.

This unexpected effect shows similarity to the observations by Li (2003) in a study on risky choices, where participants were more likely to use a heuristic of comparing extreme outcomes in the one-off condition but shifted towards maximising expected value in the repeated condition.

text.text: We propose that participants in our experiments also adopt different strategies depending on the context: Participants might rely on heuristics or intuition in the one-off condition, whereas in the repeated condition, they may anticipate the need to balance predictions over time, leading to a more rational approach.

In this section, we explain the definition of determinism (DET) and the reason for setting 1511 90% as one of our exclusion criteria.
This measure was developed by Marwan et al. (2007) 1512 to analyse recurrence in a sequence.
text.formatted: This measure was developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Marwan et al. (2007)</ref> 1512 to analyse recurrence in a sequence.

text.text: A high DET indicates that a large proportion of 1513 recurrent responses form repeated sequences, reflecting greater predictability in the 1514 generated outcomes.
We used this measure to identify highly repetitive response patterns 1515 that may depart from the intended random generation task.
The measure is based on the recurrence plot, which shows whether the element x i in 1517 a sequence is the same as x j .
Figure D1 shows an example of the recurrence plot for the 1518 sequence {4, 2, 1, 5, 4, 3, 2, 5, 4, 1}.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">D1</ref> shows an example of the recurrence plot for the 1518 sequence {4, 2, 1, 5, 4, 3, 2, 5, 4, 1}.

text.text: DET measures the percentage of the dots on the plot that fall on diagonal lines with length equal to or larger than 2: where l is the length of a diagonal, and C(l) is the count of the diagonal with length l.
For example, in Figure D1, there are eight diagonals of length 1 (single dots), two diagonals of length 2, and one diagonal of length 10 (the main diagonal).

This section reports analyses focusing on the starting point of mental simulation, defined as the initial value in the sampling sequence.

First, we examined an additional bias observed in the data: in several experiments, participants showed systematic tendencies in the values chosen as their first response, which we refer to as the starting-point bias.
Second, in Experiments 3 and 4, we tested whether the value provided in the one-off condition could be regarded as the starting point of the repeated condition.
These analyses were not central to our main research question and are presented as exploratory.
They should therefore be interpreted with caution and examined more systematically in future work.
In Experiment 1, we conducted an RM-BANOVA considering the domains, the starting points (whether the number is the first one or not) and their interaction as the fixed effects.
We also accounted for the random effect of subjects.
The BFs were 1/3.02, 2.80 × 10 3 and 1/9.37 for the domains, starting point and their interaction, respectively.
As indicated in these BFs, participants exhibited a starting-point bias.
Figure H1 shows that participants typically began with a relatively small value, and all subsequent numbers were distributed more evenly.

text.text: In Experiment 2, we ran the same RM-BANOVA including domain, starting point, and their interaction.
The BF for the domain was 1/9.83, again providing substantial evidence against a utility effect at the group level.

By contrast, the BF for the starting point was 1/2.61, offering no evidence of a bias, and the BF for the interaction was 1/38.86, indicating very strong evidence against an interaction between domain and starting point.
We propose that the absence of the starting-point bias observed in Experiment 2 is due to participants' tendency to begin with the most probable outcome when the distribution is non-uniform.

However, our distribution-based analysis provides a more direct test by comparing the UWS importance distributions with the Neutrality hypothesis.
The neutral distribution, estimated from the random generation task in the control domain, generally provided a better account of the observed responses than the UWS importance distributions.

This suggests that the over-representation of low-probability outcomes was already present in the absence of utility and continued to provide the better-fitting account when outcomes acquired utility.

In this sense, Experiment 2 bolsters the Neutrality hypothesis depicted in Figure1: People's sampling tendencies are primarily influenced by objective probabilities and unaffected by domain variations.

A fourth consideration concerns the large differences in DET between Experiments 3 and 4: Experiment 4 has more participants with high DET than Experiment 3.
As shown by Figure D2(B), this difference was particularly apparent near the upper boundary of the distribution (98-100%).
Such high values can arise from highly predictable response patterns (see Appendix D for examples).
These patterns may reflect simplified response strategies, such as exclusively selecting one outcome or following a predetermined response cycle, rather than independently imagining each draw.

Such strategies may arise from different approaches to the task, including attempts to reproduce expected outcome frequencies or reduce cognitive effort, although the present data cannot establish their underlying causes.
